unit.title: Serve, Return, Two Bounces
unit.summary: Legal serves (volley and drop), where it must land, return, the two-bounce rule.

lessons.title: Underhand, diagonal, behind the line
lessons.objective: Describe a legal serve position and target.

payload.prompt: Tap the correct target service box for a serve from the right side.

diagram.alt: Top-down pickleball court. A player stands at the right baseline, ready to serve.

explanation.correct: From the right side, you serve cross-court (diagonal) into the left box on the far side. That's diagonal serving.
explanation.incorrect: Serves go diagonal: from the right, aim for the far left box. Serving to the same side as you're standing is illegal.
explanation.sayThisLine: Serves are always diagonal, cross-court.

payload.prompt: You stand with your back foot over the baseline, serving.

scene.alt: You stand with a foot on or past the baseline, about to serve.

explanation.correct: Foot fault. You must be behind the baseline when you serve. Stepping on or over it is a fault.
explanation.incorrect: The baseline is sacred on a serve. Any part of your feet touching or crossing it is a foot fault.
explanation.sayThisLine: Foot fault, you were over the line.

options.text: You toss the ball low
You hit it below your waist with an upward motion
You hit it while crouching
You use a slice grip

explanation.correct: Underhand means the paddle contacts the ball below your waist and the motion is upward. It's a rule, not a style.
explanation.incorrect: The rule is about paddle contact: below waist, upward motion. It controls the serve's speed and style.
explanation.sayThisLine: Underhand serve is below the waist and moving up.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I'm on the right side. Do I serve to the right box?

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: No, serves go diagonal. You serve to the far left box.
Yes, you serve to the right.
It depends on the score.
You can serve to either box.

payload.translation: Pickleball serves are always diagonal (cross-court). Know this one rule and you're ahead of beginners.

followUps.line: No, serves are always diagonal. You serve cross-court to the far side.
followUps.why: Clear and definite; names the rule.

followUps.line: Diagonal! Right side serves to the far left box.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Diagonal serves are one of the clearest rules; you can be confident here.

lessons.title: The volley serve, in detail
lessons.objective: State the three volley-serve requirements incl. 2026 'clearly'.

payload.prompt: Which is a legal volley serve requirement?

options.text: The paddle head must be above the wrist
Contact must be below the waist with an upward arc
The serve can be hit overhand
The ball can be in your hand when you hit it

explanation.correct: Three requirements: paddle head below wrist, contact below waist, and upward arc. The 2026 wording: each must be 'clear'.
explanation.incorrect: All three have to be true: below-wrist grip, below-waist contact, and upward arc. Even borderline serves are faults in officiated play.
explanation.sayThisLine: Volley serve has three rules: below the wrist, below the waist, upward motion.

payload.template: The paddle head must stay {{above_or_below}} the wrist, contact must be {{above_or_below}} the waist, and the arc must be {{direction}}.

explanation.correct: Below wrist, below waist, upward arc. Remember all three or the serve is a fault.
explanation.incorrect: The rules keep serves controlled: no slamming, paddle stays compact, and motion is upward.
explanation.sayThisLine: Below the wrist, below the waist, moving up.

payload.prompt: Put the volley-serve checklist in order (how an official sees it).

items.text: Paddle head is not above the wrist
items.why: Checked first: the grip and arm position.
Checked second: where the ball is struck.
Checked third: the motion at contact.

explanation.correct: An official looks at grip, then contact height, then motion. All three have to be 'clear' per 2026 rules.
explanation.incorrect: The three checks happen in sequence: paddle position, then ball contact point, then the direction of swing.
explanation.sayThisLine: The three-part volley-serve check keeps it fair.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: My serve looked okay, but they called it a fault.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Was it close to the rules? Borderline serves are faults now.
That's just bad officiating.
You probably stepped over the line.
Don't worry about it.

payload.translation: The 2026 wording is strict: 'clearly below wrist', 'clearly below waist', and an 'upward arc'. Borderline is a fault when officiated.

followUps.line: Borderline serves are faults in officiated play. Was your motion clearly upward?
followUps.why: Explains the rule and asks a specific question.

followUps.line: Could have been the paddle position or the contact height. The 2026 rules tightened it.
followUps.why: Acknowledges the change without dismissing her.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You don't need to diagnose the fault; just remind her of the rule.

lessons.title: The drop serve
lessons.objective: Explain why the drop serve is allowed at any height and what changes.

payload.prompt: What is the key difference with a drop serve?

options.text: You can hit it from any height, as long as it bounced first
You must drop it with no upward propulsion
It doesn't count on the first try
You have to serve from behind the baseline

explanation.correct: Drop serve: release the ball, let it bounce, then hit it. You can serve from any height, making it easier than a volley serve.
explanation.incorrect: Drop serves have the same landing rules as volley serves (diagonal, in the box, past the kitchen), but you have more freedom on the height.
explanation.sayThisLine: Drop serve is easier because you can hit it from any height.

payload.title: Choosing a serve style
payload.setting: You're learning to serve and you have to pick a style.
payload.scenario: You can throw a volley serve (hit while holding the ball, below waist, upward motion) or a drop serve (drop it, wait for the bounce, then hit). Both land in the same box and count the same way.

options.text: Start with drop serve; it's easier and you can find your groove
options.outcome: Smart move. Drop serve removes one layer of complexity (the underhand grip) so you can focus on aim and landing. Volley serve comes later.

options.text: Go straight to volley serve; that's what the pros do
options.outcome: Ambitious, but drop serve is the easier way in. Pros use volley serves, but beginners find drop serve more reliable.

explanation.summary: Both serves have the same rules for landing, but drop serve has fewer moving parts. Master the aim first, then add the grip.
explanation.sayThisLine: Drop serve is the shortcut to a reliable serve.

payload.prompt: You drop the ball and it bounces. You step over the baseline, then hit it.

scene.alt: You stand over the baseline after dropping the ball; it is bouncing and you are about to hit it.

explanation.correct: Foot fault. Even on a drop serve, you must be behind the baseline when you make contact with the ball.
explanation.incorrect: The baseline rule applies to both volley and drop serves. Step over it and it's a fault.
explanation.sayThisLine: Foot fault: you crossed the baseline.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: Drop serve is so much easier. I'm just gonna use that.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Smart move. It's a totally valid way to serve.
But the pros use volley serves.
You'll have to learn volley eventually.
Drop serve is cheating.

payload.translation: Drop serve is 100% legal and equally respected. If it works for her, it works. No pressure to switch.

followUps.line: Drop serve is totally legit. Lots of players stick with it their whole career.
followUps.why: Affirms her choice without false comparisons.

followUps.line: Go for it. Same rules for landing, just easier form.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Don't shame her for using drop serve. It's a valid choice at all levels.

lessons.title: Aim it, land it
lessons.objective: Land a serve in the correct diagonal box past the kitchen line.

payload.prompt: Your serve lands right on the kitchen line on the far side.

scene.alt: Ball marking the kitchen line on the far court.

explanation.correct: Short serve. The kitchen line is part of the kitchen, so landing on it is a fault. You must clear the kitchen line.
explanation.incorrect: The kitchen line on a serve is the boundary; landing there is short. It has to be past the line to be good.
explanation.sayThisLine: Landing on the kitchen line is a short serve.

payload.prompt: Your serve clips the net cord and lands in the correct service box.

options.text: It's a let, replay the serve
The serve is good, play on
It's a fault
You get to choose

explanation.correct: No service lets in pickleball. A serve that clips the net but lands in is live, and play continues.
explanation.incorrect: Tennis has lets; pickleball does not. Net cord on a serve that lands in? Play on.
explanation.sayThisLine: No service lets. If it clears and lands in, it counts.

payload.template: A legal serve must land past the kitchen line and within the {{area}}.

explanation.correct: The serve must land in the diagonal service box on the far side, past the kitchen line. Lines are in.
explanation.incorrect: The landing zone is the service box. Anything outside it or in the kitchen is a fault.
explanation.sayThisLine: Serve must land in the service box, past the kitchen.

lessons.title: Return of serve
lessons.objective: Know the return must bounce and why deep is smart.

payload.prompt: What is the rule about the return of serve?

options.text: You must volley it back
It must bounce on your side before you hit it
You can hit it in the air if you want
There is no return rule

explanation.correct: The return must bounce first (two-bounce rule). You cannot volley the serve; you have to let it land and bounce.
explanation.incorrect: Like the serve, the return is locked by the two-bounce rule. Let it bounce, then hit it.
explanation.sayThisLine: You have to let the return bounce.

payload.title: Where to aim your return
payload.setting: You are returning the serve and you have to pick a target.
payload.scenario: The serve lands near the baseline on your side. You can hit it back: either a short return toward their kitchen, or a deep return toward their baseline.

options.text: Hit it deep, toward their baseline
options.outcome: Smart. A deep return gives you time to move up and reach the kitchen line. Short returns put you at a disadvantage.

options.text: Hit it short, near their kitchen
options.outcome: Tempting, but you lose your advantage. Deep returns buy time and position. Short returns let them attack immediately.

explanation.summary: A deep return gives your team time to advance to the kitchen line. Short returns give the serving team an easy third-shot attack.
explanation.sayThisLine: Deep returns are the smart play.

payload.prompt: The serve lands. You volley it back in the air.

scene.alt: Serve bounces on your side and you volley it in the air before it has bounced.

explanation.correct: Fault. You volleyed the return, but it must bounce first. The two-bounce rule applies to both serve and return.
explanation.incorrect: Returns, like serves, must bounce. You have to let the bounce happen before you can hit it.
explanation.sayThisLine: The return has to bounce first.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: My returns always land short. They're destroying me on the third shot.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Try aiming deep instead. It gives you time to get to the kitchen line.
That's rough. Keep trying.
Just hit it harder.
Returns aren't that important.

payload.translation: Deep returns are a strategy, not just luck. Aiming deeper changes the whole rally.

followUps.line: Deep returns give you time. Short returns let them attack right away.
Try aiming for the far baseline instead of short. Changes everything.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: This is solid advice: deep returns are the foundation of good return play.

payload.prompt: Serve just landed. It's your partner's turn to move forward.

scene.alt: Serve has landed on the far side; your partner is moving forward from the baseline.

explanation.correct: Bounce first. The serve just landed; the return still has to bounce on your side before your team can volley.
explanation.incorrect: Two bounces happen first: serve on far side, return on your side. Only after both bounces can anyone volley.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two-bounce rule means serve and return both have to bounce.

payload.prompt: Put the opening sequence of a rally in order.

items.text: Serve lands on the far side
items.why: Rally always starts with a serve.

items.text: Return is hit after bouncing on the serving side
items.why: Second action: receive and return the serve.

items.text: Third shot is hit after return bounces on the far side
items.why: Both bounces must happen now; serving team makes the third shot.

items.text: Now anyone may volley (outside the kitchen)
items.why: Two bounces done; the game opens up.

explanation.correct: Serve, return bounce, third-shot bounce, then volleys. The two-bounce rule is why the third shot is so important.
explanation.incorrect: The sequence is locked: serve, return, third, then free play. Master this and the rest makes sense.
explanation.sayThisLine: Serve, return, third shot, then you can volley.

payload.prompt: Why does the two-bounce rule exist?

options.text: To slow down the game
To keep the serving team from rushing the net immediately
To make the game fair for beginners
No particular reason

explanation.correct: The two-bounce rule forces the serving team to stay back and advance strategically, not just charge the net.
explanation.incorrect: Without the two-bounce rule, the server could volley everything and dominate. The rule evens the fight.
explanation.sayThisLine: The two-bounce rule stops the server from smashing it away.

payload.template: The {{shot1}} must bounce on the {{side1}}, the {{shot2}} must bounce on the {{side2}}, then anyone may volley.

explanation.correct: Serve bounces on the far side, return bounces on the near side. Both sides must see a bounce before volleys.
explanation.incorrect: Two bounces, one on each side: that's the rule. After that, the game is open.
explanation.sayThisLine: One bounce each side, then you can volley.

lessons.title: Serve faults, sorted
lessons.objective: Sort serve faults from legal serves; hear 'fault!' and know why.

payload.prompt: Which is NOT a serve fault?

options.text: Stepping over the baseline while serving
Serving overhand
Hitting the ball before it bounces (drop serve)
Clipping the net and landing in the service box

explanation.correct: No service lets: clipping the net and landing in is a good serve, not a fault.
explanation.incorrect: Foot faults, overhand, contacting above waist, and landing short or out are all faults. But net clips don't count.
explanation.sayThisLine: Net clip that lands in? It's good.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: They called a fault. Is it just the line calls or is there more to it?

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Could be a lot of things: foot fault, wrong box, landing short, overhand motion.
It's usually just the line.
If they called it, it must be right.
Just serve again.

payload.translation: Serve faults are wide-ranging: foot faults, aim (box/kitchen), landing position, and arm legality. Help her decode it.

followUps.line: Could be the line, your foot, the box, or the arm position. Ask them which one.
followUps.why: Names all the categories; encourages dialogue.

followUps.line: Serve faults have a bunch of reasons. It's worth asking what went wrong.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You don't need to diagnose it for her, just help her ask the right question.

payload.prompt: Match the serve fault to its description.

pairs.definition: Standing on or over the baseline when you serve
Landing in the kitchen or on the kitchen line
Landing in the correct box for the same side (not diagonal)
Landing outside the baseline or sideline

explanation.summary: Foot faults, short serves, wrong boxes, and out-of-bounds are the main fault types. No service lets is not a fault.
explanation.sayThisLine: Foot, short, wrong box, out of bounds—those are serve faults.

payload.title: The serve got called a fault
payload.setting: Sam is frustrated about a serve call.

exchanges.theirMessage: They called my serve a fault. I have no idea why.

replies.text: Did you ask which one? Foot, short, wrong box, or something else?
replies.theirResponse: Oh, good idea. I'll ask next time.
replies.coachNote: You named the categories; that's helpful.
Sympathetic, but a question would help more.

replies.text: Serves don't have that many rules. They probably made it up.
replies.theirResponse: Wow, okay. They're not making it up.
replies.coachNote: Serves have many rules. Don't dismiss the call.

exchanges.theirMessage: What are all the things that make a serve a fault?

replies.text: Foot fault, landing short in the kitchen, wrong box, or out of bounds. Also overhand or contacting above the waist.
replies.theirResponse: Okay, that makes sense. That's a lot.
replies.coachNote: You gave her the list. That's solid.

replies.text: A bunch of things. Just try again.
replies.coachNote: Give her the actual list next time.
You know the serve rules; share them.

payload.closingNote: Serve faults come down to five things: foot position, ball landing spot, box accuracy, arm legality, and (no net lets). Know these and you can decode any fault call.
